title: 投票年龄上下限
full_query: Debate whether there should be age limits - minimum or maximum - for voting. Consider democratic principles, cognitive development and decline, intergenerational equity, and the balance between inclusivity and informed decision-making.

pointwise.title: Debate over a minimum age
pointwise.question: Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a minimum voting-age limit?

anchors.1: No debate about a minimum age limit.
anchors.2: Only a position or slogan is offered.
anchors.3: A substantive reason is given on one side, but the opposing case is absent or merely a label.
anchors.4: Both sides have relevant reasons, with a minor ambiguity about the proposed limit or its implication.
anchors.5: Both the case for and the case against a minimum age limit are identifiable and reasoned, including a fair statement of a case the author ultimately rejects.

pointwise.boundary: This checks whether competing reasons are present, not whether they are equally convincing. No particular age cutoff, argument, neutral final stance or equal word count is required. Do not treat age-based stereotypes as evidence.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Debate over a minimum age': Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a minimum voting-age limit? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve a substantive supporting case for a minimum age. Preserve a substantive opposing case for a minimum age.

pointwise.title: Debate over a maximum age
pointwise.question: Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a maximum voting-age limit?

anchors.1: No debate about a maximum age limit.
anchors.2: Only a position or slogan is offered.
anchors.3: A substantive reason is given on one side, but the opposing case is absent or merely a label.
anchors.4: Both sides have relevant reasons, with a minor ambiguity about the proposed limit or its implication.
anchors.5: Both the case for and the case against a maximum age limit are identifiable and reasoned, including a fair statement of a case the author ultimately rejects.

pointwise.boundary: This checks whether competing reasons are present, not whether they are equally convincing. No particular age cutoff, argument, neutral final stance or equal word count is required. Do not treat age-based stereotypes as evidence.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Debate over a maximum age': Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a maximum voting-age limit? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve a fair supporting case for a maximum age, not the official stereotypes as facts. Preserve a substantive opposing case for a maximum age.

pointwise.title: Democratic principles
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how the proposed limits engage democratic political rights and legitimate participation?

anchors.1: No democratic-principle discussion.
anchors.2: Democracy or rights are invoked without explaining the connection to voting limits.
anchors.3: A principle is stated but how it supports or challenges an age rule is materially unclear.
anchors.4: A relevant principle is linked to an age rule with only a minor interpretive gap.
anchors.5: The report explains the relevant political-equality, participation, legitimacy or other democratic principle and how an age-based inclusion/exclusion rule engages it.

pointwise.boundary: A principle and its application form one requirement; do not require a particular theorist, constitution or predetermined conclusion about all democracies.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Democratic principles': Does the report explain how the proposed limits engage democratic political rights and legitimate participation? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Retain the relevance of political rights to age-based exclusion and assess the argument separately. Preserve the connection between age limits and democratic standards. Retain democratic voting-rights relevance without declaring a worldwide essential-right hierarchy.

pointwise.title: Cognitive development
pointwise.question: Does the report discuss cognitive development relevant to younger people's voting decisions, with its scope made clear?

anchors.1: No cognitive-development discussion.
anchors.2: Only a stereotype about immaturity or a brain-maturity age is given.
anchors.3: Specific developmental abilities are described, but their population, decision context or uncertainty is materially unclear. A generic individual-variation caveat cannot replace discussion of developing decision, impulse-control and emotional-regulation functions.
anchors.4: Relevant developmental abilities and their limits are clear, with minor context gaps.
anchors.5: Discusses developing decision-making, inhibitory control and emotional regulation, including prefrontal/executive-system development where supported; relates their different timelines to deliberative voting and individual variation rather than assigning one universal brain-completion age.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed prefrontal-cortex completion age or identical maturation timetable is required. Presence of an appropriately scoped discussion is checked here; the inference from abilities to a legal cutoff is compared separately.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Cognitive development': Does the report discuss cognitive development relevant to younger people's voting decisions, with its scope made clear? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve scoped development relevant to voting, not one universal brain-maturity endpoint. Capacity uncertainty belongs with the developmental/aging claim; policy uncertainty belongs with the policy judgment it limits. Keep individual variation in both age-related discussions and the group-to-individual inference. v3.3 restores specific executive-function content while retaining uncertainty about a single maturation endpoint.

pointwise.title: Cognitive aging
pointwise.question: Does the report discuss cognitive aging relevant to voting, including variation and the limits of generalizing from age?

anchors.1: No cognitive-aging discussion.
anchors.2: Only an old-age stereotype or uniform decline claim.
anchors.3: Specific cognitive changes are discussed but variation or their voting-relevant scope is materially unclear. Saying some people decline is insufficient if fluid processing/problem-solving/working-memory changes and retained learned knowledge are not distinguished.
anchors.4: Relevant changes and variability are clear, with minor scope omissions.
anchors.5: Explains fluid abilities such as processing speed, novel problem-solving and working memory alongside crystallized knowledge/skills and experience, with domain and individual variation; neither a fixed mid-60s onset nor lifelong immunity of learned knowledge is assumed.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require decline to start in the mid-60s or knowledge never to decline. Specifying a dimension's evidence and limits is more important than a fixed age assertion.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Cognitive aging': Does the report discuss cognitive aging relevant to voting, including variation and the limits of generalizing from age? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve aging abilities and variation while rejecting a mandatory mid-60s onset. Capacity uncertainty belongs with the developmental/aging claim; policy uncertainty belongs with the policy judgment it limits. Keep individual variation in both age-related discussions and the group-to-individual inference. Retain distinctions among aging abilities, not never-declining crystallized intelligence as a universal rule. v3.3 restores concrete fluid/crystallized distinctions rather than allowing a generic variability statement.

pointwise.title: Intergenerational equity
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how voting-age limits affect the political voice and interests of different generations?

anchors.1: No intergenerational discussion.
anchors.2: Only mentions young versus old interests.
anchors.3: A cohort effect is identified, but whose voice or interests are affected and how is unclear. A voice argument without considering how cohort sizes or an aging/youthful population alter that effect remains at most 3.
anchors.4: The age rule's effects on generations are concrete, with minor temporal or representation ambiguity.
anchors.5: The report identifies how an age rule changes generational representation or exposure to policy consequences, without treating a cohort's preferences as uniform. Explains how aging populations or youth-heavy structures can change the scale of representation effects, without assuming uniform preferences within a cohort.

pointwise.boundary: No population projection, policy example or assertion that one generation deserves more votes is mandatory. The age rule and who it affects are one relation.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Intergenerational equity': Does the report explain how voting-age limits affect the political voice and interests of different generations? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Separate whether cohort effects are described from their additional interpretive value. v3.3 restores population-structure content directly.

pointwise.title: Inclusivity and informed decisions
pointwise.question: Does the report explicitly address the tension between broad participation and informed voting?

anchors.1: Neither objective is discussed.
anchors.2: Only one objective is named, or both are slogans.
anchors.3: Both objectives are discussed but their tension or possible compatibility is not explained.
anchors.4: The relationship between participation and informed decisions is clear, with a minor unresolved term.
anchors.5: The report explains how restricting or expanding age eligibility bears on both objectives, including where they conflict or can be jointly supported.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require competence testing, civic education, epistocracy or a compromise position. This is the presence of the requested relationship, not a separate quality score for each value.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Inclusivity and informed decisions': Does the report explicitly address the tension between broad participation and informed voting? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Retain the requested inclusivity–informed-participation relation and trade-off, not a mandatory citation quota.

pointwise.title: Traceability of empirical and legal claims
pointwise.question: Can important claims about cognition, voting law or policy effects be located in specific supporting sources?

anchors.1: Central empirical/legal claims have no identifiable sources.
anchors.2: Only generic references to experts, science or law.
anchors.3: Sources are listed, but important claims' particular bases remain ambiguous.
anchors.4: Important claims have identifiable sources, with minor attribution gaps.
anchors.5: Important empirical/legal claims are clearly assigned to sources, while the author's normative premises and inferences are identifiable as such.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require a URL, medical organization or named author. A moral premise need not have a scientific citation; a neuroscience source cannot by itself establish the world's legal rules.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Traceability of empirical and legal claims': Can important claims about cognition, voting law or policy effects be located in specific supporting sources? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve appropriate legal support when a legal assertion is actually made, not compulsory assertion of universal absence. Preserve specific and applicable aging evidence, without a named researcher or fixed onset claim.

pointwise.title: Support within the verified sample
pointwise.question: Within the recorded verification sample, do cognition and voting-policy assertions match the obtained evidence?

anchors.1: A central assessed assertion is contradicted or has no claimed basis.
anchors.2: Several important assessed assertions misstate cognitive trends, laws or policy effects.
anchors.3: Support is mixed, with important scope or attribution errors remaining.
anchors.4: Assessed assertions are supported with only minor imprecision.
anchors.5: All assessed assertions match the evidence's population, jurisdiction, date and claim strength; this is not a full-report fact guarantee.

pointwise.boundary: Record selected/assessed counts and source locations. Retrieval failure is an execution issue to retry/report, not a quality score or proof of no law. This draft does not perform external verification.

provenance.change_note: Locally add 'Support within the verified sample' for this query: Within the recorded verification sample, do cognition and voting-policy assertions match the obtained evidence? The five anchors and boundaries are local design, not verbatim official reuse.

pointwise.title: Internal consistency of positions
pointwise.question: Are the report's definitions, factual statements and stated age-rule positions internally consistent?

anchors.1: Core positions contradict each other so the proposed rule cannot be identified.
anchors.2: An unexplained key contradiction changes who would be enfranchised.
anchors.3: A substantive local contradiction remains but the main positions are identifiable.
anchors.4: The main positions are consistent with minor easy-to-resolve ambiguity.
anchors.5: Definitions, factual ranges and the author's positions agree, with opponent arguments or conditional cases clearly distinguished.

pointwise.boundary: A debate may fairly state opposing positions without contradiction. Do not confuse changing assumptions with inconsistency or score normative truth here.

provenance.change_note: Locally add 'Internal consistency of positions' for this query: Are the report's definitions, factual statements and stated age-rule positions internally consistent? The five anchors and boundaries are local design, not verbatim official reuse.

pointwise.title: Non-stereotyping language
pointwise.question: Does the report argue about voting eligibility without using demeaning age stereotypes in its own voice?

anchors.1: The core case relies on demeaning labels for an age group.
anchors.2: Repeated disparagement substitutes for reasons in important passages.
anchors.3: A local substantive argument uses an age stereotype, while the main debate remains reasoned.
anchors.4: One careless or loaded expression remains but is not used as a basis for exclusion.
anchors.5: The report uses precise, non-demeaning language; attributed examples of prejudice are clearly distinguished from its own position.

pointwise.boundary: Raw official weight 21 is -4: biased language is negative. Do not penalize quoting a stereotype in order to analyze or reject it, or a forceful reasoned policy criticism.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Non-stereotyping language': Does the report argue about voting eligibility without using demeaning age stereotypes in its own voice? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Raw weight is -4: disparagement is negative, not a requested argument. Distinguish adoption from critical quotation.

pointwise.title: Existing eligibility arrangements
pointwise.question: Does the debate give a scoped factual baseline for minimum and maximum voting-age arrangements?

anchors.1: No institutional baseline.
anchors.2: Only an unscoped age or claim about all democracies.
anchors.3: Gives some minimum-age practice but not meaningful variation or the distinction from maximum-age restrictions. A clear maximum-age account with minimum-age practice or its variation missing also scores 3.
anchors.4: Explains common minimum-age practice, lower-age variations and the status of age ceilings in the jurisdictions discussed, with minor dating/scope gaps.
anchors.5: Provides a dated, sourced baseline covering the common 18-year threshold and lower thresholds such as 16 where supported, and distinguishes age ceilings from other eligibility/capacity rules; avoids a worldwide negative assertion based on a few countries.

pointwise.boundary: No mandated country list or claim that no exception can exist; a sourced correction is allowed. This is a baseline for debate, not a requirement to research every constitution.

provenance.change_note: Minimum and maximum practices are one eligibility baseline; a clear minimum with no age-ceiling distinction remains 3. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Alternatives to chronological exclusion
pointwise.question: Does the debate examine a concrete alternative for supporting informed participation without relying solely on an age limit?

anchors.1: No alternative considered.
anchors.2: Only names civic education or testing.
anchors.3: Explains an option but not how it addresses informed participation or its inclusion costs.
anchors.4: Explains a concrete option and its main trade-off, with minor implementation conditions missing.
anchors.5: Explains how an alternative such as accessible information, civic education, supported participation or a capacity-based proposal addresses the stated problem and what it may fail to solve; evaluates rather than automatically endorses it.

pointwise.boundary: No particular alternative is compulsory. No competence-test recommendation is preferred. Mere mention cannot replace consideration.

provenance.change_note: A strong age-limit argument can omit alternative means entirely; restore this independent policy-content entry. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Participation and legitimacy consequences
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain how age rules could change actual participation, representation and democratic legitimacy?

anchors.1: No practical participation consequences.
anchors.2: Only says democracy benefits or suffers.
anchors.3: Identifies inclusion/exclusion but does not explain effects on turnout, representation or public acceptance.
anchors.4: Explains the main participation-to-representation consequences and their legitimacy implications, with minor context gaps.
anchors.5: Explains how eligibility changes alter who can participate and potentially turnout, representation and perceived legitimacy, distinguishing eligible-population changes from turnout-rate changes and predictions from observed effects.

pointwise.boundary: No predetermined negative effect or required numeric estimate; the participation-to-legitimacy relationship is distinct from abstract rights and intergenerational distribution.

provenance.change_note: An elegant equality principle does not establish practical participation consequences; restore the concrete pathway. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Legal route and rights constraints
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain the legal and rights-based constraints on changing voting-age eligibility?

anchors.1: No legal or rights implementation discussion.
anchors.2: Only says a law must change.
anchors.3: Names legislation or discrimination but not how current rules constrain the proposed change. A clear legal-change route with rights constraints absent, or a clear rights discussion with no legal route, also scores 3.
anchors.4: Explains relevant legal-change and rights constraints in a stated setting, with minor scope gaps.
anchors.5: Distinguishes altering statutory eligibility from constitutional requirements where relevant, and explains how equality, age-discrimination or voting-rights safeguards constrain justification and implementation; states jurisdictional limits.

pointwise.boundary: No legal drafting exercise or universally required constitutional amendment. This evaluates a rule's feasible legal route, not abstract principle consistency in PW.D3.principle.

provenance.change_note: A clear policy preference with no implementation constraints is independently incomplete; legal route and rights barriers delimit the same change. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Institutional and social context
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain why the impact of an age rule may differ across political, cultural and economic settings?

anchors.1: No context variation.
anchors.2: Only lists countries or labels democracies emerging/stable.
anchors.3: Identifies a contextual difference but not its consequence for age eligibility or informed participation.
anchors.4: Explains relevant contextual mechanisms and their policy implications, with minor comparison limits missing.
anchors.5: Explains how education/information access, institutional protections or social and political conditions alter the impact of the same age rule; distinguishes institutions and evidence from stereotypes about emerging or established democracies.

pointwise.boundary: No compulsory country pair or causal claim that emerging democracies are less informed or more racially concentrated. Demographic cohort size is assessed in PT.D1.generations.

provenance.change_note: A demographic comparison can be strong while institutional transfer is unexplained; context-to-impact is its own relation. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Risks of eligibility screening
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain how voting qualifications could produce arbitrary or discriminatory exclusion, and assess the relevance and limits of that risk for the rules considered?

anchors.1: No discussion of screening abuse.
anchors.2: Only claims tests are fair or unfair.
anchors.3: Identifies a relevant exclusion risk or example, but does not explain how the rule or its application produces exclusion or how it bears on the voting qualification considered.
anchors.4: Explains a concrete exclusion mechanism and its relevance to the rule considered, with a minor applicability or scope gap.
anchors.5: Uses a concrete, reasoned account of a qualification rule or its implementation to explain how arbitrary or discriminatory exclusion could occur, and states the conditions and limits of applying that reasoning to the age rule or competence test considered.

pointwise.boundary: Historical evidence, an institutional analysis or an explicitly hypothetical scenario can support this item; no historical example, country, statute or date is mandatory. Identify the mechanism rather than merely label a rule discriminatory. Separate factual examples from hypotheticals and do not treat an imagined abuse as an observed event. No requirement to equate all age limits with past racial exclusion, endorse screening, or reject it. General statements of rights belong to PT.D1.democracy/implementation; this item checks how exclusion could arise through a rule or its application.

provenance.change_note: Review 36: allow concrete institutional reasoning or explicit hypotheticals as well as historical cases; preserve the exclusion mechanism and its applicability limits, not a mandatory historical route. Keep the original ID for traceability.

anchors.1: A gives a slightly more defensible capacity-to-eligibility inference; B may still be better locally.
anchors.2: A gives a substantially more defensible account of what age-related evidence implies for individual eligibility; B's local strengths do not make up for the difference.
anchors.-2: B gives a substantially more defensible account of what age-related evidence implies for individual eligibility; A's local strengths do not make up for the difference.
anchors.-1: B gives a slightly more defensible capacity-to-eligibility inference; A may still be better locally.

pairwise.boundary: Identify the inferential step from group evidence to individuals or policy. Biological maturation, health, education and political disagreement are not interchangeable measures of voting competence. No age or testing policy is preferred by default.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'From cognition to eligibility': Which report more convincingly reasons from cognitive evidence to what an age rule can and cannot establish about voting competence? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Keep individual variation in both age-related discussions and the group-to-individual inference.

Use demographic structure only through its effect on representation and fairness.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Policy trade-offs and feasible alternatives': Which report better helps assess the practical trade-offs of the age-limit positions or alternatives it actually considers? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Capacity uncertainty belongs with the developmental/aging claim; policy uncertainty belongs with the policy judgment it limits.
